answer:
Final natural-language hypothesis — NLSY79 cohort wealth comparison, 1985-1996.

Across the 1985 -> 1996 NLSY79 wealth waves, using NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC respondents (cohort code 3) as the supplied proxy for the 'white' comparison group, median family net wealth in nominal dollars of the survey year is ordered NBNH > BLACK > HISPANIC in every wave, and the disparity between the white-comparison cohort and each minority cohort widens monotonically across the window. The white-comparison median is 2.19x the Black median and 7.00x the Hispanic median in 1985 ($3,500 vs. $1,600 vs. $500; available-case N = 5,774 / 1,699 / 2,631), 2.70x and 8.11x in 1990 ($12,972 vs. $4,800 vs. $1,600; N = 5,336 / 1,528 / 2,431), and 4.35x and 16.62x in 1996 ($42,600 vs. $9,800 vs. $2,563; N = 3,557 / 1,368 / 2,114). The white-to-Black gap nearly doubles (2.19x -> 4.35x) and the white-to-Hispanic gap more than doubles (7.00x -> 16.62x) across the eleven-year span. A complete-case sensitivity panel restricted to respondents with non-missing wealth in all three waves (N = 5,739; Black 1,084 / Hispanic 1,723 / NBNH 2,932) reproduces the same ordering and the same widening trajectory (Black contrast: 2.38x -> 3.60x -> 4.69x; Hispanic contrast: ~12x -> ~12x -> 17.75x). Because all figures are in the nominal dollars reported at each interview and no CPI/deflator adjustment has been applied, part of the nominal widening mechanically reflects economy-wide price and wage growth between 1985 and 1996; the within-cohort ranking is preserved on both the available-case and complete-case views.

Caveats carried with this hypothesis. (a) The 'white' cohort is the supplied NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC proxy (code 3) — not strictly identical to non-Hispanic white. (b) Wealth is family-level (R plus spouse/family unit, assets minus debts), not per-capita. (c) Cohort fixed at the 1979 interview; no reclassification. (d) Nominal dollars of the survey year; no inflation adjustment. (e) Headline uses within-wave available cases; complete-case reported only as sensitivity. (f) Descriptive only; no median-difference test or covariate adjustment. (g) Differential attrition by 1996 (overall missingness 44.5%; ~52.7% NBNH vs ~31.7% Black / ~33.3% Hispanic) is mitigated but not eliminated by the complete-case sensitivity.

payload.hypothesis: Across the 1985 -> 1996 NLSY79 wealth waves, using NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC respondents (cohort code 3) as the supplied proxy for the 'white' comparison group, median family net wealth in nominal dollars of the survey year is ordered NBNH > BLACK > HISPANIC in every wave, and the disparity between the white-comparison cohort and each minority cohort widens monotonically across the window. The white-comparison median is 2.19x the Black median and 7.00x the Hispanic median in 1985 ($3,500 vs. $1,600 vs. $500; available-case N = 5,774 / 1,699 / 2,631), 2.70x and 8.11x in 1990 ($12,972 vs. $4,800 vs. $1,600; N = 5,336 / 1,528 / 2,431), and 4.35x and 16.62x in 1996 ($42,600 vs. $9,800 vs. $2,563; N = 3,557 / 1,368 / 2,114), so the white-to-Black gap nearly doubles (2.19x -> 4.35x) and the white-to-Hispanic gap more than doubles (7.00x -> 16.62x) over the eleven-year span. A complete-case sensitivity panel restricted to respondents with non-missing wealth in all three waves (N = 5,739; Black 1,084 / Hispanic 1,723 / NBNH 2,932) reproduces the same ordering and the same widening trajectory for both minority contrasts. Because all figures are in the nominal dollars reported at each interview and no CPI/deflator adjustment is applied, part of the nominal widening mechanically reflects economy-wide price and wage growth between 1985 and 1996 rather than only relative shifts in the wealth distribution. payload.workflow: 1. Inputs: data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61). Key columns: 'Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979' (codes 1=BLACK n=2,002; 2=HISPANIC n=3,174; 3=NBNH n=7,510) and 'Family net wealth, 1985' / 'Family net wealth, 1990' / 'Family net wealth, 1996 (key data point)' (the 1996 header carries the literal suffix). 2. Headline — within-wave available case: per-cohort median family net wealth computed on rows with non-missing wealth in that wave (negatives and zeros retained); per-cohort N, P25/P75, share of respondents with non-positive wealth reported alongside. 3. Within-wave ratios: R_black(w) = M_NBNH/M_BLACK, R_hispanic(w) = M_NBNH/M_HISPANIC, with 1/R also reported. 4. Complete-case sensitivity: same pipeline restricted to the 5,739 respondents with non-missing wealth in 1985, 1990, and 1996 (cohort counts 1,084 / 1,723 / 2,932). 5. Output: cohort ordering NBNH > BLACK > HISPANIC preserved on every wave of both views; the headline nominal white-to-minority gap widens monotonically across 1985 -> 1996; complete-case sensitivity confirms the trend (small-base wobble at 1985 Hispanic is documented). 6. Caveats: nominal dollars (no CPI), NBNH-as-white proxy, family-level wealth, cohort fixed at 1979, within-wave available-case handling, descriptive only, mildly differential attrition by 1996.
